clue.text: Light device not normally smear able

indicators.note: something not arranged normally is out of its usual order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gadget for light that, unusually, cannot smear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not normally' tells you to rearrange SMEAR ABLE, giving the nine letters of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A laser produces a narrow intense ray of light, so its output is a light device in the clue's loose sense.

clue.text: Marie takes the dolly mixture!

indicators.note: a mixture stirs things up, so the letters of the word dolly are jumbled

explanation.surface: A girl called Marie helps herself to a bag of sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: Dolly mixtures are a British sweet of small coloured pieces; here 'mixture' is the anagram signal on DOLLY. Marie Lloyd was a famous British music-hall singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Marie Lloyd was the celebrated music-hall star, so her first name points to the surname.

clue.text: Unsmocked, inert or inefficient

explanation.surface: A description of someone without a smock who is also idle and useless.
explanation.walkthrough: A shift is an old word for a smock or loose undergarment, so to be without one is to be unsmocked.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking a shift means without a smock-like garment; the everyday sense means lazy, lacking drive or resourcefulness.

clue.text: Piper's profession?

parts.note: the Pied Piper of Hamelin's job was catching rodents, so his trade is described as hunting them

explanation.surface: A question about what a piper does for a living.
explanation.walkthrough: The Piper is the Pied Piper, who rid Hamelin of rats; a dog or person that hunts rats is said to have done this.
explanation.definitionFit: To hunt and kill vermin rodents is the trade of the Pied Piper, a rat-catcher.

clue.text: Existence has its ups and downs just the same

indicators.text: has its ups and downs just the same
indicators.note: in a down clue the word reads identically going up or going down, a palindrome

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Life has its highs and lows, but stays the same.
explanation.walkthrough: ESSE reads the same both ways, so in a down entry its 'ups and downs' are identical.
explanation.definitionFit: Esse is the Latin and philosophical term for being or essential nature.

clue.text: One who gets his pennyworth for nothing?

definitions.text: One who gets his pennyworth for nothing?

parts.words: One who gets his pennyworth for nothing?
parts.note: plays on the phrase 'a penny for your thoughts': someone who can learn your thoughts without paying the penny

explanation.surface: A bargain-hunter who always gets his money's worth free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A penny for your thoughts' offers a penny to hear what someone is thinking; a person who knows them already gets that pennyworth free.
explanation.definitionFit: A telepath learns people's thoughts without being told, saving the proverbial penny.

clue.text: The baker's rounds?

parts.note: rounds suggests a delivery route, but the round things a baker makes are small loaves

explanation.surface: A question about the route a baker delivers on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rounds' suggests the baker's delivery route; it is the small round loaves he bakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Small individual loaves of bread are round items a baker turns out.

clue.text: Material for a madly gay town coat!

definitions.text: Material for a madly gay town coat!

parts.words: Material for a madly gay town coat!
parts.note: plays on the idiom 'paint the town red', to celebrate wildly, as though the town were literally given a coat

explanation.surface: Advice on fabric for a flamboyant coat to wear in town.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'paint the town red' is to go out and celebrate wildly; the coat is a coat of paint, not clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrating wildly is 'painting the town red', so the material needed is crimson colouring.

clue.text: Where the police let us go in Midlothian

definitions.text: Where the police let us go in Midlothian

parts.words: Where the police let us go in Midlothian
parts.note: refers to the tongue-twister 'The ... police dismisseth us', a test of sobriety naming a port near Edinburgh

explanation.surface: Asking which Scottish town's police released us.
explanation.walkthrough: The old tongue-twister 'The Leith police dismisseth us' was used to test whether someone was drunk; Leith is Edinburgh's port, in Midlothian.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edinburgh port district is the place named in the sobriety tongue-twister about police dismissing people.

clue.text: The root of all evil for weightwatchers ?

definitions.text: The root of all evil for weightwatchers ?

parts.words: The root of all evil for weightwatchers ?
parts.note: turns the proverb about money being the root of all evil into a literal crop root that sweetens food dieters avoid

explanation.surface: What dieters consider the source of all wickedness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The root of all evil' is money in the proverb; here it is a literal root from which sweetener, the dieter's enemy, is refined.
explanation.definitionFit: This crop's root is processed into table sweetener, the thing slimmers most fear.

clue.text: After a little work I get a setback from sleeping-pills

indicators.note: the word I comes after the little work, so it follows it in the answer

parts.note: op is the short form of opus, a musical work

indicators.note: a set turned back means the word set is written in reverse

explanation.surface: Someone does a bit of work and then suffers a relapse from taking sleeping pills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts I behind OP; 'back' turns SET into TES, placed after A. The surface 'setback' splits as 'set back'.
explanation.definitionFit: Opiates are narcotic drugs that induce sleep, such as sedatives taken at night.

clue.text: Does this acquaintance confirm his agreement …

definitions.text: Does this acquaintance confirm his agreement …

parts.words: Does this acquaintance confirm his agreement
parts.note: a slight acquaintance is called a '...' one, and a nod of the head also signals agreement

explanation.surface: Asking whether a casual friend shows he agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'nodding acquaintance' is someone you know only slightly; a nod of the head is also how you signal yes.
explanation.definitionFit: A slight acquaintance is a 'nodding' one, and bowing the head is the gesture of assent.

clue.text: … by signing on this line?

parts.note: the idiom 'sign on the ... line' means formally agree, carrying on the previous clue's agreement

explanation.surface: Continuing the last clue: the agreement is confirmed with a signature.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipses join this to the clue before; to 'sign on the dotted line' is to commit formally to a deal.
explanation.definitionFit: Forms mark the signature place with a broken line of points, hence 'sign on the dotted line'.

clue.text: Wordsworth's throstle was no mean one

definitions.text: Wordsworth's throstle was no mean one

parts.words: Wordsworth's throstle was no mean one
parts.note: quotes Wordsworth's 'The Tables Turned', where the singing thrush 'too, is no mean' sermon-giver

explanation.surface: A remark about a thrush in a Wordsworth poem.
explanation.walkthrough: A throstle is a song thrush. In 'The Tables Turned' Wordsworth writes of it: 'He, too, is no mean preacher', urging the reader to learn from nature.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth's line calls the singing thrush a giver of sermons, someone who teaches moral lessons.

clue.text: They are all-round prize-winning beasts

parts.note: a medal is the prize a winner receives
lions are the classic beasts, kings of the animals

explanation.surface: Champion animals that excel at everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all-round' looks like praise for versatile winners; it says the things defined are wholly circular, like large round medals.
explanation.definitionFit: Medallions are large circular medals or round ornaments, so they are entirely round.

clue.text: Variegated, like Browning's 3

explanation.surface: Multicoloured, just like the poet Browning's character.
explanation.walkthrough: 3 refers to 3-down, whose clue mentions the Piper; Browning's poem is 'The Pied Piper of Hamelin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pied means patched in two or more colours, and Browning's Piper wore such a coat.

clue.text: Put in the slippers — they carry weight in foreign travel

definitions.text: they carry weight in foreign travel

parts.note: to pack is to put items into a case or bag
mules are backless slippers

explanation.surface: Packing your slippers before a trip abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Mules are backless slippers, not just the animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Pack animals bear loads for travellers over rough country abroad.

clue.text: The family dependent might be so regarded, yet perversely bite an earl!

definitions.text: The family dependent might be so regarded

indicators.note: acting perversely means behaving contrarily, so the letters are rearranged out of their order

explanation.surface: A family servant might be kept on, though he contrarily bit a nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perversely' rearranges BITE AN EARL. A retainer is a long-serving household servant, so he is one who is kept on.
explanation.definitionFit: A family retainer is a servant kept in service, someone able to be held on to.

clue.text: Swelling the numbers already on the spike ?

definitions.text: the numbers already on the spike ?

explanation.surface: Rising tension over unpaid accounts piled on a spike.
explanation.walkthrough: Unpaid invoices were stuck on a desk spike; read as two words, the answer is 'bill owing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Swelling describes billowing sails or smoke; invoices awaiting payment on a spike are bills still to be paid.

clue.text: Support for the Royal Mail?

parts.note: the royal person is the monarch, a king
post is another word for mail

explanation.surface: Backing for the national postal service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal Mail' is the British postal service; split, it gives KING and POST. A kingpost is the upright beam in a roof truss.
explanation.definitionFit: A kingpost is the central vertical beam holding up a roof truss.

clue.text: No late passes for the performers I punished!

parts.note: the cast are the performers in a production
a student who is gated is confined to college, with no passes to stay out late

explanation.surface: An actor disciplined, denied late passes along with the cast.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'gated' is a British school and university punishment: confined to the premises, so no late passes.
explanation.definitionFit: To castigate is to reprimand severely or chastise.

clue.text: Plan for housing development

explanation.surface: A scheme to build homes.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot is a scheme or plan; it is also a piece of land on which houses are built.

clue.text: Shakespearian gunman

parts.note: names the swaggering companion of Falstaff whose name is also a firearm

explanation.surface: An armed character in a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: Pistol is Falstaff's blustering companion in Henry IV Part 2 and Henry V; the name is also a handgun.
explanation.definitionFit: The braggart in Shakespeare's history plays bears the name of a handgun.

clue.text: Should Lily be spoken of in this way as " mangy Lil '" ?

definitions.text: Should Lily be spoken of in this way

indicators.note: as here means 'in the form of', the quoted insult taken apart and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Asking whether calling Lily 'mangy Lil' is spiteful.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of MANGY LIL rearrange to the answer, and calling her that is spiteful.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking of someone with spite or malice is talking of her malignly.

clue.text: Animal goes to the wall in France

parts.note: le is French for the
mur is the French word for wall

explanation.surface: A creature heads for the wall in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in France' asks for French: 'le mur' means 'the wall'.
explanation.definitionFit: A lemur is a primate of Madagascar.

clue.text: After five I show intelligence about wine

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral five
nous is common sense or intelligence

explanation.surface: Someone shows shrewdness about wine after five o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: NOUS is British informal for practical good sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Vinous means relating to or resembling wine.

clue.text: "A to dream of, not to tell! " (Coleridge)

definitions.text: "A to dream of, not to tell! " (Coleridge)

parts.words: "A to dream of, not to tell! " (Coleridge)
parts.note: a quotation from Coleridge's 'Christabel' with a word left out, which the solver supplies

explanation.surface: A line from Coleridge about something beyond words.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in 'Christabel' reads 'A sight to dream of, not to tell!'; the missing word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in Coleridge's line is filled by the word for something seen, a vision.

clue.text: Part of a speech often repeated

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A section of a speech that gets said again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'speECH Often'.
explanation.definitionFit: To echo is to say again what was said, so echo stands for repeated speech.

clue.text: A great grey-green greasy river? Just so

definitions.text: A great grey-green greasy river? Just so

parts.words: A great grey-green greasy river? Just so
parts.note: quotes Kipling's 'Just So Stories', which describe an African river in exactly these words

explanation.surface: Describing a murky river, then agreeing with oneself.
explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's 'The Elephant's Child', one of the 'Just So Stories', the elephant goes to 'the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's Just So Stories famously describe this southern African river with those adjectives.

clue.text: One way of stopping the shooting

definitions.text: One way of stopping the shooting

parts.words: One way of stopping the shooting
parts.note: shooting suggests guns, but it is filming, which a director halts by calling 'Cut!'

explanation.surface: How to bring gunfire to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shooting' suggests gunfire; it is filming, halted when the director calls 'Cut!'.
explanation.definitionFit: A director ends a take of filming by calling 'Cut!', and editing film is also called this.

clue.text: A little fish caught in traps

indicators.note: the letters are caught up and tangled in the word traps, so they must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A small fish trapped in a net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught in' asks you to rearrange the letters of TRAPS.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprat is a small herring-like sea fish.

clue.text: It brings the stars into focus

definitions.text: It brings the stars into focus

parts.words: It brings the stars into focus
parts.note: stars suggests the night sky and a telescope, but they are stage performers lit by a lamp

explanation.surface: A telescope bringing heavenly bodies into view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stars' suggests astronomy; it means performers, picked out on stage by a strong lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre lamp throws a narrow beam to pick out the lead performers.
